items.title: ChittiOS – an OS where the agent is the driver
items.story_key: story|title:chittios an os where the agent is the driver
items.content_excerpt: A bare-metal OS, built from scratch in Rust — no POSIX, no libc, no ELF. A tiny language model runs on the silicon, and a capability-checked, audited ABI means it can plan anything and only do what it was granted. The model’s output is an untrusted plan . It never causes a side effect directly — it is parsed, grammar-constrained, capability- and taint-checked, and only then executed by deterministic native code. Above the line: stochastic. Below: deterministic. Delegation only ever narrows authority · a skill is bounded by its install-time grant, forever · prompt-injection-as-privilege-escalation is refused at the OS boundary. The shell coming up, a hosted model answering a question by calling a tool, the audit log, the hardware underneath, and an image decoded in-kernel — recorded from the running OS, not a mockup. CPU LLM inference on GGUF models — architecture-dynamic loaders (Qwen hybrid, Gemma), every mainstream quant plus sub-2-bit packs, hand-written SIMD kernels, split across every core. No cloud, no host. An in-kernel browser: HTML + CSS/flexbox layout, paint, forms, SVG, text selection and clipboard, and its own small JavaScript engine. Three decoders and a player, each validated frame-for-frame against FFmpeg and libvpx — 1080p30 on bare metal, with HLS over the network. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech through an in-kernel ONNX interpreter, fully offline — or a hosted provider if you configure one. An unforgeable capability ABI with a scope gate and an append-only audit log. Authority is always intersection(requested, granted). A full TCP/IP stack with real certificate verification against an embedded root store — pure Rust, no ring, built to run no_std. A tmux-style compositor: a resizable grid of up to eight panes, tabs you drag between them, a status bar on any edge, mouse, an editor, themes + wallpapers. Installable, signed agent packages (SOUL + skills + manifest) from a public registry, plus sandboxed wasm apps — notes, paint, slides, chess, games. Connect Model Context Protocol servers over HTTP/JSON-RPC — each remote tool registers as a native agent tool, taint-tracked. Drive the shell agent from external inboxes — Telegram live, Discord/Slack next. Every DM runs on a fresh model context. An ACPI AML evaluator drives the embedded controller for battery and AC state, a real power button, S5 poweroff, and suspend/resume that puts USB, the NIC and audio back. The panel picks the resolution: EDID → loader → kernel, with KMS backends for vi

items.title: How Public Evals Work, Where They Break, and What Should Change
items.summary: Some critiques and suggestions based on a teardown of 12 benchmarks.
items.story_key: story|title:how public evals work where they break and what should change
items.content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

items.title: Show HN: Run Mult AI Agents (Claude, Gemini, etc.) as a team of bees, maids
items.story_key: model:claude|title:run mult ai agents claude gemini etc as a team of bees maids
items.content_excerpt: 🐝 One Queen, many bees: an open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent into a hive. Schedules, event triggers, squads with review loops, a honeycomb view. No API keys. One Queen. Many bees. Your coding agents, working as a hive. A free, open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, DeepSeek Harness and Cursor Agent into a small, friendly team you can watch, schedule and steer. Every agent is a bee with a name, a face and a job. They bob while they work, doze when they are idle, and earn a new look as they climb from Bronze to Master. Sticker bees by default, maids or butlers if you like: pick a skin in Settings → Appearance. Honey bee, Maid café and the classic bee above come with the app; Butler is installed from More skins. Agent Hive is a macOS app that runs several coding-agent CLIs at once and lets them work as a team. Each agent is a bee : Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity ( agy ), DeepSeek Harness ( dsh ), Cursor Agent, or any command you like, working in its own folder. You can talk to each bee, put it on a schedule, chain bees into a relay where one writes and another reviews, or pull them into a group and let Queen hand out the work. It uses the CLIs and logins you already have, including a Claude or ChatGPT subscription. It ships no API keys, stores none, has no account and no server of its own. This downloads the latest release for your Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), puts Agent Hive.app in /Applications and opens it. With Homebrew: brew install --cask ericwang915/tap/agent-hive . You can also download the .dmg from the releases page . The app is signed and notarized by Apple. Pull bees into a group and tell Queen what you want. She picks the right bees, dispatches the work, waits for the results and sums them up. She only wakes the bees she needs, and she asks before hatching new ones. A group works without Queen too. @mention a bee and it starts right away. Leave the name out and a small, cheap model picks the bee the message is for, so the others stay asleep; a bee with nothing to add stays quiet. Stickers work both ways. A bee can hand part of the job to another by @mentioning it, for at most three hops. Up to six bees share a folder and pass work down the line. A reviewer can send its findings back to the writer until it approves, for at most three rounds. A handoff can carry a condition: write it in one sentence under "Only when" ("the conversion rate is below 5%", "

items.title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
items.summary: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.

items.title: How OpenAI’s Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast
items.summary: Learn how OpenAI built the Performance Factory, a system of Codex-powered workflows that finds and fixes performance issues to help keep ChatGPT fast.
items.story_key: model:chatgpt|title:how openai s performance factory keeps chatgpt fast
items.content_excerpt: The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap. In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day. Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production. As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains. Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories. 1. Pre-Codex . Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools. 2. Codex as a partner . items.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
items.summary: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

items.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
items.summary: OpenAI’s layered approach to adversarial distillation combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement to protect against capability extraction.
items.story_key: story|title:combatting adversarial distillation
items.content_excerpt: How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry. As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . items.title: Inside the Codex sandbox
items.summary: See how Codex runs commands on your machine while enforcing the filesystem and network limits you control across macOS, Linux, and Windows.
items.story_key: model:codex|title:inside the codex sandbox
items.content_excerpt: At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth ⁠ (opens in a new window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex ⁠ (opens in a new window) , to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control. A ⁠ (opens in a new window) sandbox ⁠ (opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠ (opens in a new window) permission profiles ⁠ (opens in a new window) , which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session. In this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end users and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows. In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile: Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks . Allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys). Disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read

items.title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
items.story_key: story|title:introducing harness adapters adapt your favorite model to your harness to improv
items.content_excerpt: Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. items.story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
items.content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. items.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
items.story_key: story|variant:mini|title:welcome inkling 2 mini cutting edge performance for your local setup
items.content_excerpt: TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost. Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release! We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware. This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones. Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384. The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights. Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages . Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed. Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate

items.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
items.content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.story_key: story|title:genie 4 is now available
items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. items.title: claude-code v2.1.330
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
  • Added commandPrinted to claude plugin install --json results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and commandFailed when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
  • Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
  • Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
  • Fixed ExitWorktree and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
  • Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
  • Fixed --continue and --resume opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
  • Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
  • Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
  • Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as node_modules
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
  • Fixed /rewind sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
  • Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
  • Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
  • Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
  • Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
  • Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (#101856)
  • Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several claude plugin commands ran at the same time
  • Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
  • Fixed incomplete backups of ~/.claude.json being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
  • Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
  • Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
  • Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and /compact
  • Fixed /context undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
  • Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
  • Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
  • Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
  • Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
  • Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
  • Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with claude -p --continue
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
  • Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after /context but before the first message
  • Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
  • Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
  • Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
  • Fixed /mcp listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", --mcp-config and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
  • Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
  • Fixed /stats counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
  • Fixed /ultrareview failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
  • Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
  • Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools
  • Fixed link reference definitions being dropped from CLAUDE.md and memory files that contain an HTML comment
  • Fixed running Monitors keeping the earlier conversation in memory until they end
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending a turn with "Prompt is too long" when a PDF larger than the context window followed a long conversation
  • Fixed the choice between two user or project agent files declaring the same name depending on the order the file search listed them
  • Fixed claude daemon logs never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
  • Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
  • Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
  • Fixed Read with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
  • Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
  • Fixed the Project instructions picker in /config showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window
  • Fixed a subagent's own subagents and forks running on the plan-mode model in plan mode under opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed WebFetch page summaries ignoring the /effort level when a gateway refuses the small fast model
  • Fixed claude -p on Google Cloud's Agent Platform ignoring --settings '{"fastMode":true}' when the model comes from ANTHROPIC_MODEL or a settings file; such runs now bill at the fast mode price
  • Fixed startup under forceLoginOrgUUID being refused after one temporary server error or dropped connection
  • Fixed claude mcp remove giving no way forward for a claude.ai connector: it now says to turn it off in /mcp or remove it on claude.ai
  • Fixed the /mcp "Connect on claude.ai" check saying "not connected" when claude.ai has a connector at the server's URL without its query
  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
  • Changed more rm commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
  • Changed deniedMcpServers name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
  • Changed claude --teleport in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with -p it exits 1 until you switch
  • Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 gives every model the full one
  • Changed skills that Claude runs with a model setting, other than context: fork skills, to leave subagents, forks, compaction and /recap on the session's model
  • Changed a subagent's model fallback to carry over: agents with no model and forks it then starts run on the fallback, and the agents they start use its Bedrock region
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed spawn-runner hooks to start while earlier ones still run, up to --hook-concurrency per orchestrator (4 by default); set it to 1 if yours can't run beside another
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Bash commands to skip the file diff when nothing needs it, so transcripts can lack it; set bashEditDiffEnabled to true in managed settings to get every diff
  • Changed self-hosted runners to stop a session's start at once, without trying other runners, when a checkout hook exits with status 108
  • Changed prompt hooks to accept model aliases such as haiku or sonnet in their model field
  • Changed /design-sync's fallback build of the reference Storybook to use only a Storybook installed in the project
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions signed in to a Claude apps gateway to be written from short notes instead of the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • [VSCode] Added /fork to fork a conversation after its last reply (#69272)
  • [VSCode] Added /workflows, which opens the agent map with running workflows
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.escapeStopsClaude setting; turn it off so Escape does not stop Claude (#91536)
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.pinPrompt setting to let your message scroll away instead of staying pinned
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.contextUsageThreshold setting for when the context indicator shows (#93036)
  • [VSCode] Added a prompt argument to the "Open in Side Bar" command for keybindings and extensions
  • [VSCode] Added Move up and Move down to a session group's menu (#98654)
  • [VSCode] Fixed VS Code opening and focusing its terminal on every prompt of a connected terminal session
  • [VSCode] Fixed copying a code block adding a trailing newline that ran the command on paste (#96976)
  • [VSCode] Fixed holding Enter on /rewind restoring files, and a double click on Remove or Delete removing a memory, MCP server or plugin marketplace, without confirmation
  • [VSCode] Fixed Enter on a question card sending your earlier answer instead of picking the focused one, and arrow keys not working after an "Other" answer; answered questions reopen on your pick
  • [VSCode] Fixed a held-down Enter key sending a half-written message or running a typed slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+A, C, V, X and Z not working in the rename box and dialogs on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+F and Ctrl+P not moving the caret in the message box on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Accept and Reject buttons doing nothing on a proposed diff moved to a new window
  • [VSCode] Fixed Accept and Reject Proposed Changes showing over the chat, the terminal tab and other files; they now show only on the proposed diff
  • [VSCode] Fixed a slow-starting Claude tab taking the keyboard away from the file you had gone on typing in
  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes and new problems being missed on macOS and Linux for files whose path contains #, ? or %20, such as a C# folder
  • [VSCode] Fixed whole-line selections counting one line too many in the selection chip, in @-mentions and in what Claude is told, and file links leaving out the last line of a range
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation forked in the panel re-running an old, unanswered prompt by itself after a window reload
  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation running the original conversation's /loop schedules a second time
  • [VSCode] Fixed /clear giving no sign that the session still runs without a newly trusted folder's CLAUDE.md and settings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dialogs closing, and losing typed text, when a text selection was dragged past their edge
  • [VSCode] Fixed advisor calls showing as "Unsupported content type" (#73499, #64158, #90471, #73637)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the session list showing no status for the sidebar chat's session (#93898)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the plan preview's Add Comment button vanishing after a fast double click on a word
  • [VSCode] Fixed long lines cut off in the Edit Notebook Cell row, permission rules squeezed in a narrow panel, hard-to-see question card marks, and menus moving the chat after a declined trust prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed signing in to an account on hold showing a generic failure instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
